title: Why Do Traffic Jams Appear Out of Nowhere?
pause_note: 'long' lists beat indices followed by a 1.5 s pause

beats: Why do traffic jams appear out of nowhere?
You crawl for ten minutes, bumper to bumper.
Then the road opens up, and there is nothing there. No crash. No roadworks. No lane closed.
So what stopped you?
Most of us blame something up ahead. A slow driver. Someone merging. A crash on the other side.
Sometimes that is true. Real bottlenecks do cause jams. But not always.
In 2008, a team of Japanese physicists built a road with no possible cause at all, just to find out.
And the jam showed up anyway.
Here is their road. A circle, two hundred and thirty metres around, marked out on a flat, empty track.
Twenty-two cars, spaced evenly, all asked to do the same thing: drive steadily at about thirty kilometres an hour.
No traffic lights. No junctions. No slow lorry. Every driver can see the car in front, and nothing else matters.
If any road should flow forever, it is this one.
For a little while, it does.
Then, within a few minutes, a knot appears.
A cluster of cars slows, stops, and waits, while the rest of the ring keeps moving.
Watch the knot, not the cars.
The cars keep going forward. They drive into the jam at the back, crawl through it, and leave from the front.
But the jam itself drifts the other way, backwards, against the traffic.
Why backwards? Look at the front. A car can only leave once the car ahead has pulled away, and that takes a moment.
Meanwhile, new cars keep arriving at the back. So the front is eaten away, the back keeps growing, and the whole knot slides backwards.
In the experiment it moved backwards at roughly twenty kilometres an hour.
That is close to the speed measured for stop-and-go waves on real motorways.
So a jam is not a thing. It is a wave, passing through the cars, the way a ripple passes through water.
And a wave needs something to start it.
Zoom in on one driver.
Nobody drives perfectly. The gap ahead grows a little, shrinks a little. Your foot eases off for a moment.
The driver behind you notices late. Human reactions take around a second, and when a surprise comes, often longer.
By the time they react, the gap has already closed more than they expected.
So they brake a little harder than you did, just to be safe.
Then the next driver brakes harder still.
Each car passes the slowdown back, and each one makes it slightly bigger.
Traffic engineers have a name for this. A queue where each follower amplifies the one ahead is called string unstable.
Far enough back, a gentle touch of the brakes can become a full stop.
If you have sat in traffic in a big city, you have been one of the links in that chain.
Nobody in it did anything wrong. Every driver made a reasonable choice. The jam came from all of those choices together.
But wait. If small wobbles always grow, why does traffic ever flow at all?
Because they only grow when the cars are close together.
With long gaps, a driver has room to absorb a slowdown. They ease off gently, and the wobble fades before it reaches the next car.
With short gaps, there is no room. Every wobble has to be passed on, and passed on stronger.
Physicists call this an instability. Below a certain density, smooth flow is stable. Above it, smooth flow cannot last.
Motorway data in their paper put that threshold at around twenty-five cars per kilometre in a lane.
That is about one car every forty metres in each lane, a spacing busy roads squeeze below all the time.
Past that point, traffic does not need an accident to jam. It only needs time.
So if the jam comes from how we drive, can different driving make it go away?
In a later experiment in Arizona, engineers repeated the ring with about twenty cars, and the waves came back, just as before.
Then they handed one car to a computer.
Its rule was simple. Don't chase the car in front. Hold a steady speed close to the average, and let the gap ahead grow and shrink.
That one car soaked up each wave like a sponge.
In their best run, the swings in speed around the ring dropped by about eighty per cent, and fuel use fell by about forty.
Even the number of cars getting round the ring went up, by as much as fourteen per cent.
One calm car out of twenty changed the whole ring.

You can do a small version of this yourself. Leave a longer gap. Ease off early instead of braking late. Keep your speed steady instead of closing every gap. On a busy road others may cut in, so the effect is smaller, but it still helps.
You will not get home sooner. But the drivers behind you might.
So, why do traffic jams appear out of nowhere?
Because they are not things in a place. They are waves, made by many drivers reacting a little late and a little too hard.
Once the road is crowded enough, any small wobble can grow into a full stop, travelling backwards through the traffic.
And when you finally reach the front and the road opens up, the jam is still there. It has just moved on to the drivers behind you.
Have you ever been stuck in a jam with no cause? Tell me where in the comments.
